entities.name: Peking University
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Peking University (北京大学, Běijīng Dàxué — commonly Beida), founded in 1898 as the Imperial University of Peking during the Hundred Days Reform of Emperor Guangxu, is China's oldest modern research university and the intellectual birthplace of Chinese communism, the May Fourth Movement, and modern Chinese literature. The university's role in 1919 May Fourth Movement — whose student protests at Peking University catalyzed a national cultural revolution that rejected Confucianism in favor of science and democracy — makes it the most politically consequential campus in Chinese history.

The university was established by the Guangxu Emperor as part of his 100-day reform program, modeled on Western universities, to modernize China. After the Boxer Rebellion and Qing restoration destroyed the original reforms, Peking University was reorganized in 1912 under the Republic and in 1916 brought progressive president Cai Yuanpei, who invited anarchists, liberals, Marxists, and Confucians to debate freely — the 'hundred schools of thought' moment of modern China.

Li Dazhao (university librarian) and Chen Duxiu (dean of letters) founded the Chinese Communist Party Study Group at Peking University in 1920 — with Li employing a young Hunan library assistant named Mao Zedong. Chen's New Youth magazine published Lu Xun's 'Diary of a Madman' (1918), the first modern Chinese literature work in vernacular language, launching Chinese literary modernism. The 1989 Tiananmen Square protests began at Peking University and ended 200 meters from its gates.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Peking University was the intellectual birthplace of Chinese communism — Li Dazhao's library assistant Mao Zedong absorbed Marxism here — and the 1919 May Fourth Movement that rejected Confucianism for science and democracy was the cultural revolution that made 20th-century China possible.
